endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: It is essential to address these cases equitably by identifying which subgroups are more susceptible to data gaps, finding ways to address these gaps, and managing care coordination efforts for individuals lacking key data necessary for appropriate risk categorization.

evidence.title: Characterising user engagement with mHealth for chronic disease self-management and impact on machine learning performance
evidence.outcome: ML exacerbation prediction performance by user engagement level (data sparsity)
evidence.effect: Performance was better for the most engaged users; the decrease for less frequent users was mostly offset when they engaged more near exacerbation. 60.3% engage frequently; 18.4% show transitional engagement.
evidence.quote: Machine learning performed better for users who engaged the most, however, this performance decrease can be mostly offset for less frequent users who engage more near exacerbation.

evidence.title: Clinical Context Is More Important than Data Quantity to the Performance of an Artificial Intelligence-Based Early Warning System
evidence.outcome: Performance in subgroups with more missing laboratory data (moderate/low CCI)
evidence.effect: Moderate/low-CCI patients had more missing data, but within event cohorts missingness patterns were similar and model discrimination stayed robust.
evidence.quote: Within the event cohorts, however, the high-CCI and moderate/low-CCI groups showed similar proportions and patterns of missing values.

evidence.title: Performance of PREVENT Cardiovascular Risk in Electronic Health Record-Based Clinical Practice
evidence.outcome: Calibration under missing laboratory and vital sign data across subgroups
evidence.effect: Missingness was greater among underserved groups (TC missing 52.2%); calibration was worse in the relaxed cohort especially among disadvantaged subgroups.
evidence.quote: However, calibration was worse in the relaxed cohort, especially among disadvantaged subgroups (Black patients, higher ADI quartiles, and those with Medicaid or no insurance), suggesting missingness is associated with poorer calibration even when discrimination is preserved.

evidence.title: Demographic shortcuts as marker-free backdoors: silent subgroup underdiagnosis that only operating-point audits detect
evidence.outcome: Audit blindness to patients with unrecorded race
evidence.effect: Harm reached patients whose race was never recorded; an audit on recorded demographics is blind to 30% of studies.
evidence.quote: Harm reached patients whose race was never recorded, through the pixel shortcut rather than the chart entry, so an audit on recorded demographics is blind to 30% of studies.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether identifying data-poor subgroups and managing their AI-supported care changes model performance or patient outcomes. Two of three hazard studies found that missing data concentrated in disadvantaged groups and was linked to worse calibration or to audit blind spots, while the third found that discrimination held despite more missingness.

perspectives.view: No study evaluates the recommended practice, so the rating is no direct evidence. The three supplied studies document the hazard using offline designs at evidence levels 4 and 5. Their findings are inconsistent, with two reporting the hazard present and one reporting it absent. These studies describe the problem and do not test the remedy.

In a cohort of 406,230 patients, missingness was greater among underserved groups, with one laboratory measure (TC) missing in 52.2% of cases. Calibration was worse in the relaxed cohort, most of all in disadvantaged subgroups. Miscalibration may place patients in the wrong risk tier. No study shows whether a subgroup process catches these errors before they reach patients.

One offline study found that patients with moderate or low comorbidity burden had more missing laboratory data, yet missingness patterns within event cohorts were similar and discrimination held. Read alongside the calibration findings, this suggests that the amount of missing data alone may not flag affected subgroups. Checking calibration as well as discrimination may be needed. No study reports workflow burden.

A benchmark across 7 cohorts found that harm reached patients whose race was never recorded. An audit based on recorded demographics was blind to 30% of studies. A subgroup identification process that relies on recorded race or ethnicity may therefore miss the patients whose data are least complete.

The recommendation rests on a single endorsement, the CHAI Responsible AI Guide, which states it at the must level. No regulatory or statutory source was supplied that requires health systems to identify data-poor subgroups or to coordinate their care.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares health systems or units that identify subgroups with missing or poor-quality data and set up care-management processes for them against those that do not. Such studies should measure calibration by subgroup, rates of incorrect risk categorization, time to appropriate care, and staff burden. They should also test methods for finding affected patients when demographic fields such as race are unrecorded.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Among the hazard studies, one reported greater missingness in underserved and disadvantaged groups and one focused on racial and ethnic minority populations, but none reported results specific to Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Health systems serving these groups have no evidence on whether the recommended process works for their patients.
